title: Multimodal Retinal & Optic Nerve Imaging: A Clinical Guide
summary: A comprehensive comparative analysis of retinal and optic nerve imaging modalities, focusing on the diagnostic utility of Fluorescein Angiography (FFA), Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF), and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT).

sections.title: FFA: The Gold Standard for Vascularity
Red Flags: When to Immediate Action
content: FFA: History of anaphylaxis to fluorescein (Requires premedication/crash cart)
OCT: Sudden drop in RNFL thickness (Rule out acute compressive neuropathy)
FAF: 'Target' sign in hydroxychloroquine toxicity (Immediate cessation)
OCT Macula: Subfoveal fluid in wet AMD (Urgent Anti-VEGF)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Interpretation
content: FFA: Hyperfluorescence is caused by staining, pooling, or leakage; hypofluorescence by block or filling defect.
FAF: Hyper-AF implies metabolic stress (e.g., active atrophy border); Hypo-AF implies RPE cell death.
OCT: Always correlate the 'red' and 'green' maps in ONH analysis with the actual B-scan to rule out artifacts (segmentation errors).
OCT: EDI-OCT (Enhanced Depth Imaging) is mandatory for evaluating choroidal thickness.

content.explanation: Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal (The normal order of RNFL thickness thickness in a healthy eye).

sections.title: Evidence-Based Landmark Studies
sections.content: For macular edema, the DRCR.net protocols highlight OCT as the primary guide for anti-VEGF injection frequency. For ONH analysis, the OHTS (Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study) established the diagnostic baseline for early glaucoma detection using early versions of OCT/HRT.
